No network access here, so I'll have to rely on pure static analysis. I want an answer file drafted early, so I'm sketching the skeleton while I work through the first query, `is_null() & ~is_in([1], nulls_equal=True)`. The first conjunct, `is_null`, classifies as Null nullability and comes back Opaque; the second, the negated `is_in`, goes through the negation branch for the IsIn case.

I'm checking how `has_value_constraint` treats a non-empty disallowed set, since that's what makes the filter collapse to false. The `~is_in` with `nulls_equal=True` should keep null rows, but this path marks them as rejected, which looks like the wrong call. The `drops_nulls` check also skips disallowed sets, so I want to see whether that exclusion is intentional.

I'm weighing whether the fix belongs in `classify_negation`: either skip registering a disallowed set when `nulls_equal` is true, or match only the `nulls_equal: false` case. The value-based checks, like `x == 1 & ~is_in([1])` going unsat, stay valid for non-null values, so I'd want to keep those intact.

I'm trying to pin down which routine is responsible for the wrong call. `resolve_deferred` is where the "null-required column with any value constraint is unsat" decision lives, and it relies on `has_value_constraint`, which is only called from there. `model_and_chain` calls `resolve_deferred` twice, once on the constraints and once on `before`, so that's the full set of callers I'd need to account for.

Next I'm checking whether the eager `DataFrame.filter` path, and the `with_columns` path that skips the filter rule, could hit the same wrong result. The positive `is_in` case looks fine, since null isn't in `[1]` and unsat is correct there.

Next I'm checking the remaining variants: the swapped-order and chained-filter forms should collapse into one predicate, and with `QueryOptFlags.none()` the simplification rule won't run at all. The negated membership on its own never produces an unsat, since it emits no comparison and merges to nothing.

I'm checking the remaining edge cases: a disjunction isn't handled and comes back opaque, and the `ne_missing` form also stays opaque. With `nulls_equal=False` the optimizer's unsat is correct, since the result really is empty. If the haystack contains a null, the disallowed set is dropped, so the runtime evaluation covers that case instead.

I'm checking whether `QueryOptFlags._eager` keeps `simplify_expr` on, and whether `predicate_selectivity` in `stats/node.rs` reaches `model_and_chain`, which would send an unsat result to zero selectivity.

Next I'm checking the downstream consumers that rely on this unsat result: the filter-merging step that swaps the predicate for a literal false, and whether a false-literal filter gets collapsed to an empty frame later on. I'll also look at the ordering simplification for the `sort("x")` followed by `when(x > 1)` query.

I'm tracing the ordering pass in `simplify_ordering` for the ternary case: the truthy and falsy branches are scalar literals, so their observable orders come out empty. The mask `x > 1` is added after that accumulation, and since deordering isn't allowed at the top level, the output ends up with no observable order. That leaves the Select with no order-observing input, so the Sort underneath gets unlinked, which explains why the output follows the unsorted input order.

Checking the ordering pass now: the deorder branch clears the observable order for the mask node, which looks suspicious even though the main problem is the top-level output calculation.

I'm questioning whether the mask-deordering line is also off: when deordering is allowed, returning empty for the mask could still be fine, but I need to check how the Select's input order gets set when the output has no observable order.

I'm checking whether the ternary's mask gets folded into the output's observable order: the snapshot is taken before the mask is added, so the Select ends up with no order-observing input and the Sort beneath it gets dropped.

I'm checking the ordering pass for the ternary case. The mask is added to the accumulator after the output's observable order has already been snapshotted, so the Select ends up with no order-observing input.

I'm checking the string-label variant and the streaming path next, since both run the same optimizer pass with the order-observe flag on. The `QueryOptFlags.none()` setup turns that flag off, so it's a different case. The eager `DataFrame` version has no sort node in its plan at all, since the sort runs immediately. The `then(pl.col("x"))` branch is the one that differs, because a column reference counts as an observed order, so the select keeps its input ordering.

Now I'm checking how the head(3) pushes down: the slice gets moved into the Sort node by slice pushdown, which is why the ordering pass sees a sorted input that still gets dropped.

The head(3) pushdown matters here: the slice moves into the Sort node, so it survives the unordered-output check and the sort still runs, giving [0, 1, 1].

I'm checking the projection pushdown on the join: the `x >= y` predicate needs `y`, which isn't in the projected columns, so the filter has to keep that column alive through the join.

I'm checking how the join's projection pushdown treats the suffixed `k_right` column: it traces back to the right-side `k`, so the right input only needs `y` and `k`. Since `k` no longer collides with a left column, the output names come out as `x`, `y`, `k`, which means the `k_right` reference has to be renamed away.

Still tracing the join projection: `k_right` should resolve back to the right-side `k`, but the values I'm seeing look like `y`, so the suffix mapping is what I need to check.

I'm now checking the projection pushdown on the join: the `x >= y` predicate pulls in `y`, so the join has to keep that column alive even though `select("x")` doesn't ask for it. The output still seems to carry `y`, which points to something in how the projected names get computed before the output schema is replaced.

I'm going to read the start of the pushdown function, the section covering the projected-names helpers and post-projection, to see how a Select sitting above the join gets handled.
